drills.q: Explain why a unit test with a mocked database cannot substitute for a real-database integration test, with a concrete bug example.
drills.a: A mock only proves your code calls the driver in the expected way; it can't catch a wrong SQL join, a real constraint violation, a driver serialization mismatch, or actual locking/transaction interactions. Example: a JOIN that silently produces duplicate rows due to a missing condition passes against a mock returning canned data but fails against a real database enforcing real relationships.

drills.q: Describe the transactional-rollback isolation pattern for Postgres integration tests and explain why it's both fast and safe.
drills.a: Each test runs inside a database transaction that is rolled back at teardown instead of committed. Writes are fully real within the test (constraints enforced, queries see them), but invisible to every other test once rolled back. It's fast because rollback is a near-free operation compared to truncating tables or restarting a container per test, while still exercising the real engine.

drills.q: A parallel CI run of an integration suite is flaky about 1% of the time; the same suite run serially is always stable. Diagnose the root cause and the fix.
drills.a: Parallel workers are likely sharing one container/database/schema without per-worker isolation, so concurrent writes from different tests race or collide non-deterministically. Fix: give each parallel worker its own schema or its own dedicated container instance, rather than adding retries which would just mask the underlying isolation bug.

drills.q: Why can't the transactional-rollback isolation pattern be used as-is for Kafka, and what's the actual isolation mechanism used instead?
drills.a: Kafka has no free transactional rollback like a relational database -- once a message is produced it's committed to the log. Isolation instead requires explicit per-test teardown: deleting and recreating topics, using unique topic names per test, or resetting/tracking consumer group offsets deliberately.

drills.q: Explain the Testcontainers 'singleton container' pattern, why teams use it, and its main risk.
drills.a: One container instance (e.g. a Postgres container) is started once via a static initializer or session-scoped fixture and reused across an entire test class or suite, amortizing the 1-3 second startup cost instead of paying it per test. The main risk is state leakage between tests if a rigorous isolation mechanism (transaction rollback, truncation, or unique per-test schemas) isn't layered on top of the shared container.

drills.q: A team substitutes H2 for Postgres in their 'integration tests' to make them faster. Explain concretely why this is a red flag rather than a reasonable optimization.
drills.a: H2 diverges from Postgres in SQL dialect (window functions, JSONB operators, ON CONFLICT upserts) and in isolation/locking semantics. Tests can pass against H2's approximation while the exact same logic fails against real Postgres in production -- exactly the class of bug integration tests exist to catch, defeated by the substitution.

drills.q: An integration suite passes reliably on a developer's laptop but times out intermittently in CI. Walk through the triage order and identify the most common wrong fix.
drills.a: First check whether the test polls for actual container readiness (real connection/health check with retry and backoff) rather than a fixed sleep() -- CI runners are commonly slower/colder than local Docker. Then check CI runner CPU/memory limits throttling the container, then Docker-in-Docker overhead if CI itself runs containerized. The common wrong fix is increasing a fixed sleep duration, which only shifts the flakiness threshold rather than removing the underlying race.

drills.q: A service depends on Postgres, Redis, and Kafka. Design an integration test strategy that stays fast as the suite grows to hundreds of tests.
drills.a: Start all three as session-scoped containers once per suite rather than per test. Apply the cheapest correct isolation per system: transaction rollback for Postgres (near-free), explicit flush/reset for Redis, and unique topic names or explicit recreate/cleanup for Kafka (no free rollback for either). Reserve tests exercising all three systems together for genuinely cross-system behaviors (e.g., an outbox pattern), pushing single-system logic down to faster, narrower integration tests against just that system.

drills.q: Explain what's wrong with a shared fixtures.sql file loaded once for an entire integration test suite, even though it seems more efficient than per-test seeding.
drills.a: Tests end up implicitly depending on specific rows and values existing in the shared dataset without that dependency being visible in the test itself. Any change needed by one test (adding a row, changing a value) risks silently breaking other tests that assumed the old shape, and the failure's actual cause is only discoverable by reading the shared fixture file -- not the failing test. Per-test factory-based seeding keeps each test's actual data dependencies self-documenting and immune to other tests' needs changing.

drills.q: When is it correct to accept a slower, container-per-test integration test pattern instead of the faster session-scoped-container-plus-transaction-rollback default?
drills.a: When the code under test needs a genuinely fresh schema or database state that a rolled-back transaction can't provide -- the clearest example is testing database migrations themselves, where the test needs to apply schema changes against a clean instance. Accepting the slower runtime for that narrower subset of tests is correct rather than forcing migration tests into the same isolation pattern used for ordinary read/write logic tests.
